blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Recent neural implicit and Gaussian splatting approaches have achieved impressive results in multi-view surface reconstruction. However, jointly optimizing geometry and appearance introduces ambiguities. A parametric appearance model can compensate for geometric errors, reproducing the input images accurately without an accurate surface. We demonstrate accurate neural implicit surface reconstruction using only multi-view patch photoconsistency with geometry-based visibility, without volumetric rendering or parametric appearance models. For each reference ray, sphere tracing computes the first surface intersection. Its position and normal define a local patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across visible neighboring views using colors sampled directly from the input images. For efficient sphere tracing, we use a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron. We use a single photoconsistency loss, without foreground masks or auxiliary geometric regularization. Experiments show that our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BlendedMVS (BMVS) among compared methods and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Reconstructing a surface from multiple calibrated images is a fundamental problem in 3D vision. Multi-view stereo (MVS) has traditionally recovered geometry through image matching and geometric consistency [ 11 , 33 ] . Neural implicit representations have subsequently become a standard tool, providing continuous, resolution-independent representations of geometry. Early methods optimized signed distance or occupancy fields through differentiable surface rendering [ 45 , 29 ] . Later approaches, including NeuS [ 38 ] and VolSDF [ 44 ] , adopted volumetric rendering, converting the implicit representation into a density and accumulating colors along camera rays. More recently, 3D Gaussian splatting [ 20 ] has enabled efficient rendering using explicit Gaussian primitives. Geometry-oriented variants, including 2DGS [ 15 ] , PGSR [ 4 ] and AmbiSuR [ 22 ] aim to improve surface reconstruction while retaining opacity-based compositing along camera rays. In these methods, photometric supervision is applied to rendered images rather than directly to the reconstructed surface, potentially allowing geometric inaccuracies to persist (Fig. 2 , top). Moreover, parametric appearance models, such as color MLPs or spherical harmonics, can compensate for geometric errors by adjusting the predicted appearance. Methods such as NeuralWarp [ 6 ] and Geo-NeuS [ 10 ] address these limitations by introducing explicit multi-view patch photoconsistency alongside volumetric rendering, improving geometric accuracy. This raises the question of whether patch photoconsistency alone can provide sufficient supervision to optimize a continuous neural surface, without volumetric rendering or a parametric appearance model. To investigate this question, we directly optimize a continuous neural surface through multi-view patch photoconsistency, building on the principle of photometric agreement between corresponding image regions [ 8 , 37 , 11 ] . Specifically, we represent the surface as the zero level set of a 1-Lipschitz MLP and use sphere tracing [ 14 ] to compute the first surface intersection along each camera ray (Fig. 2 , bottom). At each intersection, the surface position and normal define a local tangent-plane patch whose photoconsistency is evaluated across neighboring views, with visibility explicitly determined from the evolving surface geometry. Colors are sampled directly from the input images through differentiable interpolation, without a parametric appearance network. Since patch photoconsistency relies on sufficiently accurate initial correspondences, existing methods start from a sparse set of matched keypoints [ 11 ] or refine an existing reconstruction [ 37 , 6 ] . Similarly, we initialize the implicit field from a coarse geometric proxy obtained by classical MVS from the same input images, then refine its zero level set using only multi-view patch photoconsistency. Our method achieves the lowest mean Chamfer distance on BMVS and matches the geometric accuracy of leading reconstruction methods on DTU. The main contributions of this paper are: 1. A geometry-only optimization formulation of neural surface reconstruction based solely on multi-view patch photoconsistency, without
volumetric rendering, a parametric appearance model or
auxiliary geometric regularization. 2. A differentiable first-hit optimization framework that explicitly evaluates source-view visibility against the evolving neural surface.

blocks.en:
Neural surface reconstruction. Neural implicit methods represent geometry as the level set of a signed distance or occupancy field and optimize it by comparing rendered colors with observed images, typically using a parametric appearance model. Colors are evaluated either at the first surface intersection [ 45 , 29 ] or, following NeRF [ 28 ] , integrated along camera rays [ 38 , 44 ] . Later
work improves geometric detail and
representation capacity [ 23 ] .
To address the geometric ambiguity of photometric rendering, several methods introduce additional constraints. MVSDF incorporates stereo-derived depth and feature consistency [ 46 ] , while NeuralWarp and Geo-NeuS combine volumetric rendering with patch photoconsistency [ 6 , 10 ] . Geometry-oriented Gaussian splatting methods [ 15 , 4 , 22 ] similarly add geometric constraints to opacity-based rendering.

blocks.en: Differentiable surface rendering. Optimizing implicit surfaces through ray intersections requires both differentiating the intersection points and computing them reliably. Differentiable surface rendering methods propagate gradients through these intersections using implicit differentiation [ 45 , 29 ] or approximate sphere-tracing gradients [ 24 ] . Other approaches address visibility discontinuities through reparameterization [ 36 , 3 ] . Sphere tracing [ 14 ] finds the first surface intersection along a ray using steps bounded by the distance to the surface. Eikonal regularization encourages SDF behavior [ 13 ] but does not guarantee such bounds, and its optimization can exhibit instabilities [ 42 ] .

blocks.en:
To complement DTU’s fixed camera trajectory (Sec. 4.3 ), we evaluate
on BMVS [ 43 ] , whose object-centric scenes provide
approximately 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} view coverage, testing our method
under more varied visibility configurations.
We evaluate on 8 8 scenes used in
prior neural surface reconstruction benchmarks, with 31 31 to 143 143 calibrated images at 768 × 576 768\times 576 resolution. Unlike DTU, BMVS uses reference meshes reconstructed from images,
without independently measured geometry or reported accuracy [ 43 ] . We follow the BMVS
protocol used by ProbeSDF [ 35 ] . Neural implicit meshes are extracted using marching cubes at resolution 512 3 512^{3} [ 25 ] . The metric is the
bidirectional unsigned point-to-surface distance between the predicted mesh and
the reference mesh. Distances larger than 0.025 0.025 in normalized
scene coordinates are discarded before averaging, and scores are reported × 10 3 \times 10^{3} . As shown in Table 1 , our method achieves the lowest mean error among all compared methods (2.02 versus 2.17 for Geo-NeuS), outperforming Geo-NeuS on five of eight scenes. The largest improvement occurs on Jade ( 3.89 3.89 vs 4.88 4.88 ), which combines the highest occlusion rate (Fig. 14 ) with intricate geometry. Removing occlusion filtering increases error on Jade to 4.20 4.20 , while enlarging patches from 5 × 5 5\times 5 to the 11 × 11 11\times 11 size used in Geo-NeuS raises it to 5.58 5.58 . This is consistent with larger patches being less well approximated by tangent planes on curved surfaces and more likely to cross depth discontinuities near thin structures.

DTU [ 17 , 1 ] provides calibrated multi-view images with structured light ground truth, for which Jensen et al. [ 17 ] report a standard deviation of
0.14 mm, measured on a sphere of known geometry. We evaluate the standard 15 scans, each containing 49 to 64 images at 1600 × 1200 1600\times 1200 resolution. We reran baselines using the official implementations and recovered their published results under their original evaluation protocols, except for Geo-NeuS (0.60 mm versus the published 0.51 mm), consistent with independent reruns reporting 0.59–0.62 mm [ 18 , 32 ] . For both rerun columns, all meshes undergo the same silhouette crop using masks dilated by 12 pixels [ 6 ] . Neural implicit meshes are extracted using marching cubes at resolution 512 3 512^{3} [ 45 , 38 ] , while Gaussian splatting methods retain their mesh extraction procedures. We sample the meshes, transform the samples to DTU coordinates, and compute bidirectional Chamfer distance CD 1 \mathrm{CD}_{1} (mm) against the official ground truth (Appendix A.4 ).

Neural implicit methods mesh the zero level set of the full field, whereas
Gaussian methods fuse depth maps rendered from the training
views [ 15 , 4 ] . Consequently, neural implicit meshes can retain more spurious geometry
in poorly observed regions (Fig. C.6 ).
We therefore apply the same visibility culling to all rerun meshes. Using only the meshes
and input cameras, a face is kept if it is unoccluded in at least five cameras
whose viewing rays make at most 75 ∘ 75^{\circ} with its normal
(Appendix A.4 ), similar to [ 40 ] . Culling mainly removes poorly observed peripheral regions (Figure C.6 ).
For our method, culling improves the accuracy term from 0.60 to
0.43 mm while leaving completeness nearly unchanged
(0.54 to 0.56 mm), suggesting the removed regions
contribute geometric errors without substantially improving
surface coverage. The resulting mean CD 1 \mathrm{CD}_{1} of 0.49 mm
nearly matches AmbiSuR (0.48 mm), which additionally
uses pretrained depth priors. Fig. 8 reports Chamfer sensitivity to the culling parameters.

blocks.en: 5.2 Visibility and depth localization

blocks.en:
To isolate the effect of visibility filtering, we fix the
reconstructed surface and estimate depth along reference rays
by minimizing the patch photoconsistency loss, with
and without source-view occlusion filtering.
We compare these estimates against depths derived from
DTU ground-truth point clouds.
Partially occluded rays are those whose ground-truth surface
points are visible from at least two and occluded from at least
two of the six selected source views.
Across 15 DTU scans, filtering reduces mean absolute depth
error from 2.81 to 2.13 mm on 83k partially occluded rays,
compared with 1.19 to 1.15 mm on 148k reliable foreground
rays. Improvements across all 15 scenes indicate that
visibility filtering primarily benefits depth localization
under partial occlusion (Table 13 ).

To assess the effect of replacing volumetric rendering with
direct patch photoconsistency, we compare our formulation
with NeuS, which uses volumetric rendering without explicit
multi-view matching. We initialize NeuS from the same coarse
surface, retaining its architecture, rendering loss and
eikonal regularization, but without foreground masks.
With matched initialization and geometry architecture,
our formulation outperforms NeuS on 14 of 15 DTU scans
(0.60 vs. 0.75 mm), while achieving the same mean accuracy
as Geo-NeuS (0.60 mm), which combines volumetric rendering
with patch photoconsistency.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We have demonstrated that accurate neural surface reconstruction does not require joint geometry and appearance optimization. By optimizing first-hit surface intersections through multi-view patch photoconsistency, our formulation avoids the coupling between geometry and appearance inherent in rendering approaches while achieving competitive or superior geometric accuracy. These results suggest that direct surface optimization is an effective alternative to volumetric rendering with appearance models for neural surface reconstruction.
As an extension, photometric bundle adjustment [ 7 ] ,
alternating between camera pose and surface optimization,
reduces mean BMVS CD 1 from 2.022 to 1.896 (6.2%),
improving all eight scenes (Appendix C.4 ).
Similar pose refinement would probably also benefit other reconstruction methods. This formulation also has limitations. Photoconsistency constrains only surface regions with valid intersections and multi-view correspondences, so the method depends on initialization, although similar results from ACMMP and COLMAP initializations show that it does not rely on a particular MVS method. Omitting geometric regularization isolates what photoconsistency alone can constrain, at the cost of local roughness in some reconstructions. Normalized correlation also discards absolute intensity and contrast, motivating richer photometric matching objectives. Finally, extending the approach to larger, unbounded scenes remains future work.
